analysis.one_liner: Surtaxes billion-dollar corporations whose CEOs earn over 30 times what their median worker makes.
analysis.headline: Sole sponsor Sen. Merkley's bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on September 9, 2019, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new tax on top of the corporate income tax for companies with more than $1 billion in gross revenue where the chief executive's salary is more than 30 times the median employee's. The extra tax starts at 2% of taxable income and climbs to 10% as the pay gap widens, reaching the top bracket only when a CEO out-earns the median worker 1,000-to-1 or more. The stated aim is to give big corporations a financial reason to either pay their middle workers more or pay their top executives less.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large corporations would benefit in two ways: the tax gives their employer a direct financial incentive to raise median wages, and any revenue the surtax collects flows to the Treasury, reducing the burden on other taxpayers. Communities could also see pay gains at major local employers.

how_it_helps.text: Applies only to corporations with gross revenue over $1 billion and a CEO-to-median-pay ratio above 3,000% (30-to-1), so small businesses and companies with modest pay gaps are untouched [S3].
Charges 2% of taxable income for gaps over 30-to-1, rising through tiers to 10% for gaps over 100,000% (1,000-to-1), so the penalty grows with the size of the disparity [S3].
A company could lower its bill either by narrowing the ratio through higher median wages or by reducing executive salaries; the median of all employees, not just a few, sets the denominator [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large, highly profitable corporations with extreme pay gaps would pay the surtax, and the cost would largely fall on shareholders through lower after-tax profits or on executives if companies close the gap by cutting executive pay.

drawbacks.text: The tax is defined using wages reported under section 3121 of the tax code, which excludes many forms of executive pay such as stock options, carried interest, and equity awards, so companies could restructure compensation into non-wage forms to avoid the surtax entirely [S3].

The ratio counts only employees, so a company could outsource janitorial, warehouse, and call-center work to contractors, removing the lowest-paid people from its median and shrinking its measured disparity without actually lifting anyone's pay [S3].

Taxing a ratio rather than an amount gives companies the cheapest path of cutting executive salary rather than raising worker pay, and critics of pay-ratio measures have long noted that disclosure rules have not noticeably narrowed pay gaps at covered firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is sound and targeted: it taxes only billion-dollar firms with pay gaps most people would find extreme, and it gives them a clear way out by paying workers more. Its main weakness is gaming. Because the trigger is executive wage (not total compensation) and the median counts only direct employees, sophisticated companies could likely restructure pay and outsourcing to sidestep it. The bill was a statement of principle that was never refined through committee work, so whether it would have changed real-world pay is untested.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Merkley introduced the bill on September 9, 2019 [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which was its last action of record [S5].
No other senator ever signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill received no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and was not carried over into any later legislative vehicle during the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Billion-dollar corporations with extreme CEO-to-worker pay gaps are better off, since no surtax was ever imposed, and the Senate Finance Committee preserved the status quo by never acting on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations that kept wide pay gaps

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Share for Workers Act and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the roughly 16 months after referral, leaving it to die at adjournment.

against.name: 41 other Senate Republicans and the remaining Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: None of the 99 other senators signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with no bipartisan base or path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill and not one senator from either party cosponsored it, so support never extended beyond its author.

industries.industry: Large corporations with extreme CEO-to-worker pay gaps
industries.note: These firms would owe an extra tax of 2% to 10% of taxable income, giving them a direct financial stake in avoiding it, whether by raising median wages, restructuring executive pay into non-wage forms, or outsourcing low-wage jobs. Workers benefit only if companies choose the pay-raise route.

industries.industry: Stock-option and equity-compensation planners (executive pay consultants)
industries.note: Because the tax keys off wages under section 3121, shifting executive pay into options and equity would avoid the surtax, increasing demand for exactly the compensation engineering the bill's backers view as part of the problem.
